crosswalkNote: This NE Veg. Classification V4 concept is equivalent to the V3 concept with the same name.

The Betula papyrifera/Corylus cornuta Woodland contains an open tree canopy dominated by Betula papyrifera. Shrub and herb strata are dominated by species with somewhat boreal affinities, such as Corylus cornuta, Linnaea borealis, Cornus canadensis, Disporum trachycarpum, Pyrola elliptica, Maianthemum canadense, and Aralia nudicaulis. This community is suspected to occur in boreal transition areas of southern Manitoba such as the Turtle Mountains and the Pembina Valley. References: The Nature Conservancy (1996), Lenz (1995).

An upland forest type dominated by Betula papyrifera. A number of coniferous species may also occur in the overstory in small amounts (<25% canopy cover), including Abies balsamea, Picea glauca, Picea mariana and Pinus banksiana. These forests are usually herb and shrub rich, although poor understory development is also possible. Tall shrubs may include Abies balsamea, Acer spicatum and Amelanchier spp. Low shrubs can include Diervilla lonicera, Linnaea borealis and Vaccinium spp. Common herbs may include Clintonia borealis, Cornus canadensis, Maianthemum canadense, Aralia nudicaulis and Trientalis borealis. Generally occurring on fresh to moist, coarse-textured, non-calcareous mineral soils. This forest type appears to be similar to the Betula papyrifera-(Pinus banksiana)/Rubus pubescens Forest (CEGL002513); investigation may be required to determine whether the two forests are distinct. Similar to NW Ontario FEC type V4. Reference: Sims, et al. (1989).

This forest tends to be shrub-rich, including such species as Acer spicatum, Abies balsamea, Corylus cornuta and Amelanchier spp. Development of the herbaceous layer is variable, with Rubus pubescens, Aralia nudicaulis, Cornus canadensis, Mitella nuda, and Equisetum arvense among the most common herbs. Moss cover is lower than in the related Picea glauca-Abies balsamea/Pleurozium schreberi Forest (CEGL002509), due to the dense shrub layer found here. Occurring on fresh to moist, usually well drained mineral soils. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V21 and NW Ontario FEC type V24. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Sims, et al. (1989).

stateName2: Picea glauca - Abies balsamea / Pleurozium schreberi Forest

crosswalkNote: Dominated by Picea glauca and/or Abies balsamea, often with lesser amounts of Picea mariana. The understory of this forest ranges from shrub and herb poor to moderately rich. Abies balsamea is often abundant in the tall shrub stratum, along with Amelanchier spp. Low shrubs may include Linnaea borealis, Diervilla lonicera, and Rosa acicularis. Cornus canadensis, Maianthemum canadense, Aralia nudicaulis and Clintonia borealis may be common herbs. The forest floor is covered with Pleurozium schreberi, an important feature distinguishing this forest from the related Picea glauca-Abies balsamea/(Acer spicatum)/Rubus pubescens Forest (CEGL002446). Occurring mainly on fresh, well drained, upland mineral soils, most commonly with coarse-loamy texture. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V21 and NW Ontario FEC type V25. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Sims, et al. (1989).

Picea mariana - Picea rubens / Pleurozium schreberi Forest

crosswalkNote: An upland Picea mariana forest type with a poorly developed understory and a forest floor covered with a continuous mat of mosses, including Pleurozium schreberi, Hylocomium splendens, Ptilium crista-castrensis and Dicranum polysetum. The tall shrub layer is sparse, consisting of scattered Alnus viridis [= A. crispa] and Picea mariana. Vaccinium spp., Linnaea borealis and Ledum groenlandicum are the most common low shrubs, while Cornus canadensis, Maianthemum canadense and Petasites palmatus are the most common herbs. Occurring mainly on fresh, well drained, upland mineral soils, commonly with clayey or loamy texture. Similar to Manitoba FEC types V27 and V29 and NW Ontario FEC type V33. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Sims, et al. (1989).

G102. Southern Rocky Mountain Bristlecone Pine Forest & Woodland - A0537. Pinus aristata Woodland Alliance. This is a woodland association dominated by the evergreen needle-leaved tree Pinus aristata, averaging 40-50% cover. Picea engelmannii, another coniferous tree, is present as scattered individuals. Seedlings and saplings of either species are infrequent and shrubs are absent from most stands. The herbaceous understory layer is moderately sparse, with total cover averaging <20%. The perennial forb Trifolium dasyphyllum clearly dominates, with 10-12% cover. The remaining herbaceous species are a mix of perennial graminoids and forbs; important species include the graminoids Calamagrostis purpurascens, Carex siccata, Festuca brachyphylla, and Trisetum spicatum, and the forbs Achillea millefolium, Arenaria fendleri, Penstemon whippleanus, Polemonium pulcherrimum ssp. delicatum, Sedum stenopetalum, and Solidago simplex. (NatureServe Explorer 2024)

stateName2: Pinus banksiana - (Picea mariana, Pinus strobus) / Vaccinium spp. Rocky Woodland

crosswalkNote: An open-canopied (25-60% overall tree canopy cover) woodland found on rock outcrops and dominated by Pinus banksiana and Picea mariana. Shrub and herb strata are poorly developed to absent. Species which may be present include Vaccinium spp. (V. angustifolium, V. myrtilloides, V. vitis-idaea), Juniperus communis and Arctostaphylos uva-ursi. The soil surface may be covered by an almost continuous carpet of lichens (Cladina spp., Cladonia spp.). Occurring mainly on rock outcrops or dry, rapidly drained, shallow sandy soils. Additional information is required to fully document this type and distinguish it from the Pinus banksiana/Lichen Woodland (CEGL002522). Similar to Manitoba FEC type V26. Reference: Zoladeski, et al. (1995).

stateName2: Pinus banksiana - Picea mariana / Vaccinium spp. / Pleurozium schreberi Forest

crosswalkNote: An upland forest dominated by Pinus banksiana and Picea mariana. Scattered occurrences of Picea mariana and Alnus viridis [= A. crispa] form the tall shrub stratum. The herb and low shrub strata may be quite poorly developed, with the most common species including Vaccinium spp., Aralia nudicaulis, Cornus canadensis and Maianthemum canadense. The forest floor is covered with a continuous mat of mosses, including Pleurozium schreberi, Hylocomium splendens, Ptilium crista-castrensis and Dicranum polysetum. Occurring on dry to moist, coarse to fine textured, mineral soils. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V28 and NW Ontario FEC type V32. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Sims, et al. (1989).

stateName2: Pinus banksiana - Populus tremuloides / Diervilla lonicera Forest

crosswalkNote: An upland Pinus banksiana-dominated, mixed forest often with Populus tremuloides, Picea mariana and Betula papyrifera in the tree canopy. The understorey is typically herb and shrub rich, with Diervilla lonicera, Alnus viridis [= A. crispa], Rosa acicularis, Amelanchier alnifolia and Viburnum spp. the most important tall shrubs. Low shrubs may include Vaccinium vitis-idaea, and Arctostaphylos uva-ursi. Linnaea borealis, Cornus canadensis, Fragaria virginiana, Aster ciliolatus, Rubus pubescens and Aralia nudicaulis are among the important herbs. Occurring on fresh to moist, rapidly drained, fine-textured mineral soils. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V15. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Mueller-Dombois (1964).

An even-aged Pinus banksiana forest with a variable understory. Tall shrubs tend to occur in widely-spaced clumps, and include Amelanchier spp., Alnus viridis [= A. crispa], and Corylus cornuta. The abundance and richness of low shrubs on the forest floor is a diagnostic feature of this community, with the most common species being Arctostaphylos uva-ursi, Rosa acicularis, Linnaea borealis, Vaccinium spp., and Diervilla lonicera. The herbaceous layer may include Maianthemum canadense, Elymus innovatus, Oryzopsis asperifolia, Cornus canadensis, and Lathyrus ochroleucus. Patches of Pleurozium schreberi are scattered and discontinuous. Soils are rapidly drained Podzols, with fresh moisture regime and silty to sandy particle sizes. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V24. Reference: Zoladeski, et al. (1995).

crosswalkNote: A Populus tremuloides-dominated forest, with an admixture of Abies balsamea, Picea glauca, Betula papyrifera and Picea mariana in the tree canopy (evergreen tree species making up <25% canopy cover). The understory is usually herb and shrub rich. In most cases, dense thickets of Acer spicatum and Corylus cornuta are found in the tall shrub stratum. Low shrubs may include Linnaea borealis, Rubus pubescens, Rosa acicularis, Vaccinium angustifolium, Vaccinium vitis-idaea and Diervilla lonicera. Aster ciliolatus, Aralia nudicaulis, Cornus canadensis, Maianthemum canadense and Viola renifolia may be among the common herbs. Although this type can be quite variable in its composition and structure, its main diagnostic feature is its lack of moss cover, compared with the Populus tremuloides-Betula papyrifera-Picea mariana/Alnus viridis/Pleurozium schreberi Forest (CEGL002514). Occurring on deep, moist, well drained mineral soils. Similar to Manitoba FEC types V6, V7 and V8. Reference: Zoladeski, et al. (1995).

crosswalkNote: A wet, Populus tremuloides-dominated swamp forest. Mueller-Dombois (1964) described this forest as a variant of the Larix laricina swamp forest (F134.00) found on lacustrine flats and in shallow depressions on water-modified ground moraines in southeast Manitoba. Cornus sericea [= C. stolonifera], Alnus incana [= A. rugosa], Salix spp., and occasionally Betula pumila, may form dense thickets. The herb layer may contain Carex lacustris, Glyceria striata, Caltha palustris, Petasites sagittatus, Mentha arvensis, and Galium trifidum. Soils are sandy to loamy, generally overlain by 15-20 cm of nutrient-rich, organic muck. The forest may remain flooded through June, but slow movement of the water ensures that it remains oxygenated. Confirmation and further description of this community is required before it can be ranked. Reference: Mueller-Dombois (1964).

crosswalkNote: In Delaware this maritime forest community most often occurs in places that are adjacent to salt marshes. The water table is close to the surface and the elevation is barely above that of the adjacent salt to brackish marshes. Due to the effects of salt spray and wind the canopy is shortened and trees can show stunting. Common species in the canopy include wild black cherry (Prunus serotina), sassafras (Sassafras albidum) and sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua). Other species may include serviceberry (Amelanchier canadensis) and post oak (Quercus stellata). The known examples in Delaware often have a strong understory component of northern bayberry (Morella pennsylvanica). Common greenbrier (Smilax rotundifolia) can be found in growing on the ground. Few herbs are found in this and may include (Chasmanthium laxum).

crosswalkNote: Populus tremuloides types listed in the literature are described as upland associations and are usually not considered riparian (Johnston 1987). Johnston (1987) describes various related Populus tremuloides stands: Populus tremuloides/Amalanchier alnifolia-Prunus virginiana p.a. which can have relatively abundant Acer glabrum; Populus tremuloides/Symphoricarpos oreophilus p.a.; and a Populus tremuloides/Thalictrum fendleri p.a. Hansen et al. (1988) describes a Populus tremuloides/Salix geyeriana type that contains an abundance of Cornus sericea. Walford (1994) desribes a Psuedotsuga menziesii/Acer glabrum-Pyrolia asarifolia type with Cornus sericea in the shrub layer. crosswalkNote: CEGL001473 Calamovilfa longifolia - Stipa comata ranked G3  - on 2004 and earlier tracking lists as CEAB000098 Calamovilfa longifolia - Stipa comata. Code updated to CEGL001473 in 2005. - Adams et al. 1997 recognize several different Calamovilfa - dominated grassland types, many with a strong Stipa comata component as well as a Calamovilfa longifolia - Stipa comata type.

Hansen et al. (1988, 1991) report a Spartina pectinata dominance type from central and eastern Montana, where it can form nearly pure stands in swales, meadows, and at the edges of marshes and ponds. Jones and Walford (1995) describe a community from northeastern and south eastern Wyoming. Weaver (1965) reports hundred of square miles of bottom land floodplains along the Missouri River and its tributaries covered in Spartina pectinata. A Spartina pectinata/Calamagrostis canadensis plant association has been reported from north-central Nebraska (Johnston 1987). Several Spartina pectinata co-dominated grassland plant associations have been reported from Nebraska, North and South Dakota, and Kansas (Midwest Heritage Task Force 1994). Bourgeron and Engelking (1994) list a Spartina pectinata and S. pectinata-Scirpus pungens from Colorado and Montana that may be similar.

The Fraxinus pennsylvanica-(Ulmus americana)-Acer negundo Forest has a closed canopy dominated by Fraxinus pennsylvanica, Acer negundo, and occasionally Ulmus americana (in the absence of Dutch Elm Disease). Other tree species that may occur occasionally are Populus deltoides, Quercus macrocarpa, and Tilia americana. The shrub layer may be dominated by saplings of the major tree species, along with Cornus sericea [=C. stolonifera], Ribes hudsonianum, Prunus virginiana, Viburnum lentago, Amelanchier alnifolia, Crataegus chrysocarpa, Corylus cornuta, Symphoricarpos occidentalis, Ribes americanum, Toxicodendron rydbergii [=Rhus radicans], Rubus idaeus and Viburnum rafinesquianum. The herbaceous layer can be somewhat patchy with the more common species including Laportea canadensis, Amphicarpaea bracteata, Smilacina stellata, Menispermum canadense, Galium triflorum, Vitis riparia, Osmorhiza longistylis, Urtica dioica, Parthenocissus quinquefolia, Solidago spp., Aralia nudicaulis, Stachys tenuifolia, Maianthemum canadense, Lysimachia ciliata, Smilax herbacea, Galium boreale, Aster simplex, Echinocystis lobata, Rosa woodsii and Thalictrum venulosum. Soils are cumulic regosols which lack horizon development due to periodic flooding with alluvial material. They are generally fresh to moist and have textures ranging from silty clay to silty loam. References: Marr Consulting (1995), Essenburg (1991).

SIMILAR TO STANDS DOMINATED BY SALIX MONTICOLA INCLUDED IN THE SALIX BOOTHII/CAREX AQUATILIS TYPE DESCRIBED BY PADGETT ET AL. 1989 AND YOUNGBLOOD ET AL. 1985

Padgett et al. (1989) describe a Salix boothii/mesic forb association that includes stands dominated by Salix drummondiana with Salix monticola occasionally present in small amounts. In Colorado, Salix monticola is more common and an important component in the tall shrub layer. Johnston (1987) lists a Salix drummondiana/Calamagrostis canadensis association that includes Salix monticola in the species list. Another similar association may be Salix geyeriana-Salix spp./Calamagrostis canadensis (Johnston 1987). Our stands appear to be similar to some stands included in Salix monticola/Calamagrostis canadensis or Salix drummondiana/Mertensia ciliata associations described by Cooper and Cottrell (1990) from the Colorado Front Range.

Cooper and Severn (1992) found pure stands of this type in the San Luis Valley in south-central Colorado. poorly drained basins and along pond and lake margins in shallow water. crosswalkNote: This type is based on A. Schotz observations at Eglin AFB and has later been applied to AL examples (Conecuh NF) which are being regularly burned. The placement of Splinter Hill Bog under this type is not clear. Aristida beyrichiana and Eurybia eryngiifolia (= Aster eryngiifolius) distinguish this type from more western parts of the East Gulf Coastal Plain seepage bogs (of eastern LA and MS). Eurybia eryngiifolia is rare in Alabama, and may not be present in occurrences of this association found in that state. Note that Panicum nudicaule is erroneously not regarded as a valid taxon in Kartesz (1999), and also needs a name in Dichanthelium. Examples of this association are documented at Splinter Hill Bog, Alabama.

Different sub-types of POw can have many different combinations of tree oaks, including Quercus stellata, velutina, coccinea, prinus and/or alba. Rarely tree-form blackjack oak on very clayey sites. POw1 has both pine species with post oak, POw2 has both pine species with a mixture of tree oaks, POw5 has pitch pine and post oak, POw6 has pitch pine and a mix of oaks, POw7 has pitch pine, black & post oak, POw8 has pitch pine and arborescent blackjack oak, sometimes mixed with other tree oaks. All sub-types have at least 5-25% cover of shrub oaks (shrub-form blackjack oak and/or scrub oak). POw5 often has 50-100% shrub oak cover due to thinner tree oak cover.

crosswalkNote: This association concept was originally based on one site in Cades Cove (Gum Swamp) at 535 m (1750 feet) elevation. The area is heavily browsed by deer. A similar site upslope has Acer rubrum (var. trilobum?) occurring with Liquidambar styraciflua. One of the Sphagnum species associated with these forests may be a disjunct Coastal Plain species, Sphagnum cuspidatum (= var. floridanum?) (B. Dellinger pers. comm.). More information is needed about the naturalness of these examples. The cited vegetation at Uwharrie National Forest is not actually an upland depression swamp and is thought to be successional vegetation (M. Schafale pers. comm. 2007). The status of a purported example at Duke Forest (Durham or Orange counties, North Carolina) is not known. The naturalness of vegetation at these Piedmont locations is unclear (M. Schafale pers. comm. 2001); this may represent a degraded form of ~Quercus phellos / Carex (albolutescens, intumescens, joorii) / Climacium americanum Forest (CEGL007403)$$. This association (with an expanded and generalized concept) is being utilized for a sample from the Chattahoochee National Forest (Georgia Piedmont). Data are also available from the Bankhead National Forest (Work Center Gum Pond).

crosswalkNote: Twenty-six plots (11 occurrences) represent this type in West Virginia, where it was classified as part of a 2004-2006 study of high-elevation wetlands in the Allegheny Mountains region (Byers et al. 2007). This type clusters consistently together and ordinates in a close grouping in the ombrotrophic portion of species space. The type has been adequately sampled throughout its range in West Virginia. The Virginia occurrence is probably a low-elevation (460 m) outlier of the high Allegheny type. In Virginia, beaver activity in recent years has raised water levels as much as 0.7 m in Spring Pond and has damaged, but not destroyed, the peat mats supporting this community (G.P. Fleming pers. comm.). Sarracenia purpurea (purple pitcherplant) has been introduced to this habitat in Virginia and West Virginia. This community needs to be compared to possibly related communities. It shows considerable affinities to other boggy communities with abundant Vaccinium macrocarpon (cranberry), recognized for areas north of Virginia, as well as cranberry zones in "bogs" of the Southern Blue Ridge (which have not been recognized separately in the National Vegetation Classification).

crosswalkNote: A raised bog wetland community, with an open canopy (25-60% overall tree canopy cover) of Picea mariana growing on a continuous mat of Sphagnum spp. Raised bogs (including domed bogs and peat plateau bogs) are typically higher in elevation than their surroundings and without any surface runoff, are dependent upon precipitation alone for nutrient inputs. Consequently, they are nutrient-poor, as reflected by the species-poor shrub and herb strata. Although the dominant species in raised bogs are similar to basin bogs, they seem to have a greater abundance of other dwarf-shrubs such as Vaccinium vitis-idaea, and Vaccinium oxycoccos [= Oxycoccus spp.], than do basin bogs, indicating their ombrotrophic nutrient status. Occurring on wet organic soils. Further investigation is required to allow differentiation between a number of Picea mariana-dominated forest and woodland communities. Similar to Manitoba FEC type V33. Reference: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Zoltai, et al. (1988b).

A wet, shrub-rich Picea mariana forest. Occasionally, other species such as Abies balsamea, Larix laricina, or Thuja occidentalis may appear in the tree canopy. Alnus incana [= A. rugosa] is the dominant tall shrub, along with Abies balsamea and Picea mariana. Diversity of low shrubs and herbs may be high. Ledum groenlandicum may form a dense low shrub cover, and Equisetum sylvaticum may be an abundant herb. The forest floor cover consists mainly of Sphagnum spp., with some Pleurozium schreberi and broadleaf litter from shrubs present. Occurring on wet lowland sites with deep fibric organic soils. Similar to NW Ontario FEC type V35. Reference: Sims, et al. (1989).

crosswalkNote: The Fraxinus nigra-(Ulmus americana)/Cornus sericea [=C. stolonifera]/Carex spp. Forest is dominated by Fraxinus nigra in the upper canopy, with a secondary canopy of Ulmus americana, Acer negundo, Populus balsamifera, and occasionally Abies balsamea and Picea glauca. The shrub and herb layers are usually very rich. Important shrubs include Cornus sericea, Prunus virginiana, Rubus pubescens, Acer spicatum, Alnus incana [=A. rugosa], and Ribes spp. Common herbs may include Carex spp., Calamagrostis canadensis, and Caltha palustris. Usually found as small stands along periodically flooded creeks and small rivers. Substrate may vary from saturated with pools of standing water, to drier solid ground. Substrates either deep, moist to wet, mineral soils, or organic. References: Zoladeski, et al. (1995), Zoltai, et al. (1988).

crosswalkNote: A wet, Larix laricina-dominated swamp forest, often found on lacustrine flats and in shallow depressions on water-modified ground moraines. Picea mariana, Thuja occidentalis, and Populus tremuloides may be occasional components of the tree canopy. Alnus incana [= A. rugosa], Cornus sericea [= C. stolonifera], Salix spp., and occasionally Betula pumila may form dense thickets. The herb layer may contain Caltha palustris, Petasites sagittatus, Iris versicolor, Mentha arvensis, and Galium trifidum. Glyceria striata and Carex lacustris are characteristic graminoids. Soils are sandy to loamy, generally overlain by 15-20 cm of nutrient-rich, organic muck. The forest may remain flooded through June, but slow movement of the water ensures that it remains oxygenated. Reference: Mueller-Dombois (1964).

crosswalkNote: A wet, lowland forest dominated by Thuja occidentalis, with occasional occurrences of Picea mariana, Abies balsamea, Betula papyrifera and Fraxinus nigra. Alnus incana [= A. rugosa] is the dominant tall shrub, often forming dense thickets with Thuja occidentalis. Young individuals of the other overstory tree species are also common in the tall shrub stratum. Diversity of low shrubs and herbs may be high. Ledum groenlandicum is generally a dominant low shrub. The forest floor cover consists of Sphagnum spp. in wet depressions, with Pleurozium schreberi on logs and drier hummocks. Occurring on wet lowland sites with organic soils.
